prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [adversarial] Long headers over tiny numbers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Site" · longest unbreakable word 28px · one-line width 28px
  col 2: header "Average weekly active users across all platforms" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 347px
  col 3: header "Median session length in minutes" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 238px
  col 4: header "Share of sessions that ended in a purchase" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 307px
  col 5: header "Number of support tickets opened" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 246px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 593px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 592px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"All words remain intact and the headers are readable, though the first metric has more space than it needs while the last two headers stack over four lines."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The headers remain intact, but the wide Site column leaves unnecessary space and makes the metric columns feel cramped."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"The narrow Site column leaves useful room for the metrics, and the support header fits in three lines; the other long headers still stack over four."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"The columns are reasonably balanced and all words remain intact, although all four metric headers occupy four lines."},"E":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The compact Site column gives room to the metrics; the first two metric headers fit comfortably in three lines, and all words remain intact."},"F":{"grade":"bad","why":"The narrow session-length and support columns break words into fragments, making the headers difficult to read and creating an excessively tall header row."}},"best":["E"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"C is also well balanced; the preference for E rests on its more readable session-length header and overall distribution of space."}
